endorsements.quote: Systems must support interpretation, contestability, and human override, ensuring that final decision making remains with patients and clinicians.

Addressing it requires representative data, intersectional evaluation, context specific validation, and continuous monitoring, supported by transdisciplinary input to ensure that algorithmic systems do not reinforce structural inequities in reproductive health.

This requires data minimisation, context-sensitive protections, and enforceable mechanisms that ensure meaningful user control over how reproductive data are collected, used, and shared across digital health systems.

Accordingly, accountability must be embedded through clear role allocation, continuous monitoring, and mechanisms that ensure responsibility remains traceable across all actors involved in system development and use ( 53 ).

Define clear responsibility across the AI lifecycle, require audit trails and transparency documentation, and introduce periodic review, post-deployment monitoring, and performance drift assessment ( 19 , 54 , 64 , 74 ).

Require representative and context-relevant training data, routine bias audits, intersectional performance assessment, and monitoring for discriminatory impacts across subgroups ( 16 , 23 , 33 , 57 ).

Implement privacy-first architectures, strong consent and access controls, limits on secondary use, and context-specific safeguards for sensitive reproductive data ( 17 , 42 , 63 ).

Embed participatory governance by involving affected communities, clinicians, public health experts, ethicists, and reproductive justice stakeholders in design, evaluation, and oversight ( 22 , 23 , 76 , 77 ).

unlisted_practices: Require local and external validation of AI tools, with implementation testing in intended-use settings, before deployment.
Set deployment rules that account for legal context, system capacity, and availability of follow-up care.
Treat explainability as a design requirement for AI systems, sufficient for informed and contestable use.
Do not deploy reproductive health AI systems unless minimum governance conditions are met.
Regulators should set and enforce standards for reproductive health AI, making governance obligations enforceable.
